query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases is governed primarily by the synergistic interaction between Al, Cr, and Ti at the matrix grain boundaries, which promotes selective oxidation and/or internal oxidation leading to grain boundary embrittlement. The presence of these elements at specific concentration thresholds, combined with the retained fcc structure, determines the formation and stability of protective oxide scales (e.g., Al2O3, Cr2O3, TiO2) and the susceptibility to intergranular attack.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a single-phase fcc matrix, notable strength and fatigue performance, and uniform microstructure.
generation.intervention: Elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., 800–1000°C) to oxidizing (air, O2) or reducing (H2, CO) gases for controlled durations.
generation.conditions: Temperatures between 800–1000°C; gas environments: air (oxidizing), H2 or CO (reducing); exposure times from hours to days; samples with and without grain boundary enrichment of Al, Cr, Ti.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary chemistry and microstructure, specifically the enrichment and distribution of Al, Cr, and Ti at grain boundaries within the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: Synergistic elemental effects at grain boundaries promote selective oxidation (Al, Cr, Ti) and/or internal oxidation, resulting in the formation of oxide scales and possible grain boundary embrittlement. The stability and protectiveness of these oxides depend on local composition and phase stability, which are influenced by the retained fcc matrix and additive manufacturing-induced microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with higher grain boundary enrichment of Al, Cr, and Ti will show more rapid degradation (e.g., loss of mechanical integrity, embrittlement, oxide scale spallation) during oxidizing exposure compared to samples with uniform distribution or lower concentrations. In reducing environments, internal oxidation and phase destabilization may occur, but degradation will be less pronounced unless grain boundary enrichment is present.
generation.baseline: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with uniform fcc matrix and no grain boundary enrichment, exposed to same conditions but with minimal degradation and retained mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis applies to alloys with similar fcc matrix and comparable Al, Cr, Ti concentrations; does not apply to alloys with different phase structures (e.g., bcc, intermetallics) or significantly different elemental ratios.
generation.uncertainty: Lack of direct evidence for grain boundary chemistry in this specific alloy under these conditions; synergistic effects may vary with minor compositional changes or processing history; oxide scale formation and stability may depend on additional factors (e.g., minor elements, manufacturing defects).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy samples: one with enhanced grain boundary enrichment of Al, Cr, Ti (via heat treatment or processing), and one with uniform distribution. Expose both sets to 900°C in air for 24 hours. Assess mechanical integrity (tensile/fatigue tests), microstructure (SEM/TEM), and oxide scale formation (XRD, EDS).
measurements: Oxide scale composition and thickness (XRD, SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with grain boundary enrichment do not show increased degradation (e.g., embrittlement, oxide scale instability, loss of mechanical properties) compared to baseline samples, the hypothesis is falsified.
